messages.subject: PLS % contribution of total covariation
parts:
Hello everybody,

I am hoping you can help me figure out the following: after having used the integration.test function, I would like to know the % each PLS captures of the total covariance but I am kinda stumped on what might be a good way how to go about it in R!

I was initially thinking along the lines of generating the covariance matrix of the two block (e.g. cov.il.is <-cov(il.is.int$A1.matrix,il.is.int$A2.matrix) and computing the eigenvalue for each PLS , and then regress these. But of course the cov matrix has a very different structure, so that will not work. I am clearly thinking in the wrong direction, but for now I can’t seem to see the tree in the forrest. Any ideas?

Best wishes,
Katrien

messages.author: 4d71c6e24fb21497
messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] PLS % contribution of total covariation
parts:
Katrien,

It is generally not wise to attempt an interpretation of the % covariation explained by a particular PLS axis: that is forcing PLS into a PCA-way of thinking.

With PCA, there is only one data matrix, and thus there is total variation. Here, one can consider how much is explained on each orthogonal axis and derive some interpretation. However, with PLS, there are two matrices whose covariation is being explained, and a similar logic for interpretation is not straightforward. For instance, one could have very little covariation between the two matrices, but of that little covariation, most is in the first PLS axis. Considering this at a percentage of total covariation then gives the misleading impression that the high percentage is rather impressive. It may not be.

Generally, it is best to stick with the PLS correlation for interpretation. Or better yet, interpret the empirically-derive effect size found from the observed rPLS and its permutation distribution.

Dean

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] PLS % contribution of total covariation
parts:
Hello Dean,

You are absolutely right. It was actually meant as an in-between step to calculate how much integration explains shape variation, and me using the PLS scores to achieve this. It is in this context that I thought knowing how much covariation each PLS represents would be useful, to ensure I capture say 95% in all my data sets. I hope that makes more sense now why I was interested in PLS%, and my apologies for not fully explaining the rabbit hole I found myself going down in.

Thank you for your comments on how to deal with integration interpretation, which is the part I will concentrate on now (and no doubt will prove a more fruitful pursuit).


Enjoy your day,

Katrien
